description: We’re building an Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map that maps safe routes, key hazards, and habitat zones on Mars. We turn complex space data into clear visual tools, and we’re seeking teammates in Mars research, data visualization, web development, design, and storytelling.
summary:
Redstep turns real NASA mission data into one plain answer for a Mars crew about to step outside: GO, CAUTION or NO-GO, and why.

It starts on a 3D Mars globe built from Viking colour, MOLA height and TES dust maps, USGS's 5 m CTX mosaic, Perseverance's and Curiosity's real paths, and their latest raw photos, each labelled with its mission and instrument.

Pick Jezero or Gale Crater and the planner tests every combination of science stops, choosing the most science that keeps the crew safe. It weighs slope from 40 m height grids, suit air with a turn-back point and reserve, sun height from NASA's Mars24, radiation from Curiosity's RAD, radio delay to Earth, live NASA DONKI space weather and dust-storm season. You can drag the route, plan a two-astronaut walk or add a rover drop-off.

Then you live the walk: fly it in a helmet display, follow a timed wrist checklist, and train with a survival guide that includes a Storm Risk Estimator built on 14,974 cataloged dust storms.

Why it matters: the first Mars walks will weigh science against risk with Earth light-minutes away. Redstep puts that judgement in one place and never guesses: every number is tagged NASA DATA, DERIVED or ILLUSTRATIVE, with sources listed.

Built with React, MapLibre GL, three.js and Web Workers; the core runs offline after first load. 41 automated tests check terrain, routes, air and safety rules.

An independent student entry, not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA.
details:
Redstep is a web app for exploring Mars and planning a walk at Jezero Crater. You pick a route, and it gives an instant, data-backed verdict on how safe it is, along with the science you can do on the way. It’s built from real NASA mission data and was made for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

Its benefits are that it turns complex mission data into a quick safety assessment, it ties each route to specific science, and it lets anyone explore the Martian terrain without specialist training. The intended impact is to show how public space data can make Mars exploration planning more accessible.

The page doesn’t list its tech stack. It’s hosted on Vercel and set up as a mobile-friendly web app, but I can’t confirm the framework, data sources, or any AI components.
